Survival-Supervised Bayesian Matrix Factorization for Prognostic Molecular Programs in Pancreatic Cancer

Author

Andrew Walther

Published

November 13, 2026

Summary

Aim. Bulk pancreatic tumors mix tumor, stromal and immune signals. We ask whether a Bayesian matrix factorization that lets survival inform its molecular programs can find prognostic programs that an unsupervised factorization misses, and whether its risk score transfers to new cohorts.

Method. The model factorizes expression into patient activities and gene loadings and links survival through a Cox model on the projection of each patient’s expression onto the loadings. A survival weight \(w_S\) sets how much the Cox partial likelihood is weighted relative to the expression likelihood. The primary comparator uses the same factorization at the same rank fitted without survival, followed by a Cox model on its program scores.

Results. On 273 training patients, five-fold cross-validated concordance was 0.663 for the supervised fit and 0.652 for the two-step fit. The external results in this version come from the supervised YFB fit (\(w_S = 1\), 2,218 genes, rank 7) and its two-step comparator (Section 1.6). Scored once on 5 external series, their mean concordance was 0.620 against 0.613, a pooled paired difference of +0.007 (95% donor-bootstrap interval −0.003 to 0.017). Across the gene sets, the median survival share of the loading precision of the nonempty programs was at most \(8 \times 10^{-7}\), and the supervised and unsupervised loadings correlate at 1.000. The difference is consistent with joint coefficient estimation under a shrinkage prior. That explanation was not tested separately. Against DeSurv, elastic-net Cox and PurIST, all trained on the same patients, every paired difference in mean external concordance had a 95% interval that included zero (Section 4.7). In simulation, supervision matches the two-step fit when a prognostic program is easy to find. Supervision improved recovery near the detection threshold under strong survival. Choosing the weight by cross-validated partial log-likelihood on the training data kept \(w_S = 1\), and the fit keeps all 7 programs because ELBO pruning failed its simulation criteria.

External cohorts. Every modeling choice is made by simulation and five-fold cross-validation on the 273 TCGA and CPTAC training patients. This covers preprocessing, gene screening, priors, rank, survival weight and comparator tuning. The five external expression series and the matched ICGC methylation set only score a model that is already fixed. The gene screen, the per-cohort standardization and rank 7 were set before this rule, using external concordance, and are being reselected on training cross-validation (Section 3).

Work of November 9–13. The analyses of this week compare priors on the loadings and the survival coefficients, fit methylation alone, test one fitter for several data types, compare two ways of linking survival to the programs, and reselect the gene screen, input scaling and rank on training data. Their results are in progress or pending review and appear as marked placeholders in Section 3.

1 Methods

1.1 Notation

Patients are indexed by \(i = 1, \dots, n\), genes by \(j = 1, \dots, p\) and programs (factors) by \(k = 1, \dots, K\). Patient \(i\) has observed time \(t_i\) and event indicator \(\delta_i\) (1 for death, 0 for censoring). The training data are an \(n \times p\) expression matrix \(Y\). For a random quantity \(\theta\) under the variational posterior \(q\), \(\bar\theta = E_q\theta\).

Two patient-level quantities are kept apart. The activities \(L \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times K}\) are posterior scores in the reconstruction \(Y \approx LF^\top\) and exist only for training patients. The program scores \(Z = Y\bar F\) are the product of a patient’s expression with the posterior-mean loadings. They enter the Cox predictor and can be computed for any new patient whose expression is measured on the same genes.

1.2 Model

The expression matrix is modeled as \[ y_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K L_{ik} F_{jk} + e_{ij}, \qquad e_{ij} \sim N(0, \tau_j^{-1}), \tag{1}\] with independent point-Laplace priors on the entries of each column of \(L\) and \(F\), a point mass at zero mixed with a Laplace distribution, whose parameters are estimated by empirical Bayes within each program with the R package ebnm (Willwerscheid et al. 2025). Each gene has its own residual precision \(\tau_j\). Survival follows a Cox model (Cox 1972) whose linear predictor is the program-score projection, \[ \eta_i = \sum_{k=1}^K Z_{ik}\beta_k, \qquad Z = Y\bar F, \qquad \beta_k \sim N(0, \sigma_k^2), \tag{2}\] with the prior variance \(\sigma_k^2\) estimated per program. This is the YFB model, named for its predictor \(\eta = (YF)\beta\). Because new patients are scored by the same projection, prediction needs no refitting.

The variational objective is \[ E_q \log p(Y \mid L, F, \tau) \;+\; w_S\, E_q \log \mathrm{PL}(\beta, F) \;-\; \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, \text{prior}), \tag{3}\] where \(\mathrm{PL}\) is the Cox partial likelihood. The survival weight \(w_S\) multiplies the Cox term wherever it appears: in the loading update, in the coefficient update and in the objective. At \(w_S = 1\) the objective is the evidence lower bound of the joint model. Larger values of \(w_S\) give survival more influence on the loadings. The full derivation, with every update checked term by term against the code, is in derivations/SSBMF-YFB-model-derivations/SSBMF-YFB-model-derivation-full.pdf (Appendix A).

Scale. The reconstruction does not fix the scale of a program: multiplying \(L_{\cdot k}\) by \(c\) and dividing \(F_{\cdot k}\) by \(c\) leaves \(LF^\top\) unchanged. The fit therefore rescales each nonzero program after a sweep so that its posterior mean training projection has standard deviation 1. Each \(\beta_k\) is then a log hazard ratio per standard deviation of the program score, and a single \(w_S\) means the same thing for every program.

1.3 Fitting and prediction

Each sweep re-expands the Cox partial likelihood to second order around the current \(\bar\eta\), with the predictor’s variance taken from \(q(\beta)\) and \(q(F)\). It then updates, one program at a time, the coefficient, the activities and the loadings. The loading update uses the reconstruction residual and the weighted Cox contribution to its precision and linear term. Each sweep ends by updating the noise precisions and rescaling the programs. The fit starts from the singular value decomposition of \(Y\) and stops when the relative change in the objective falls below \(10^{-5}\) or after 300 sweeps. The working fit is unpruned at rank 7 (Section 4.6).

New cohorts are standardized gene by gene within cohort and scored on the training genes they measure. The direction of the risk score is the one the fit learns from training survival. There is no post-fit sign correction: a fit oriented the wrong way would have training concordance below 0.5 and is reported as fitted.

1.4 The two-step comparator

The rank-matched comparison uses the same fitter at \(w_S = 0\), which removes survival from the loading update and gives the unsupervised empirical-Bayes factorization at the same rank, on the same genes and patients. Because \(w_S\) also multiplies the Cox term in the coefficient update, \(w_S = 0\) gives \(\beta = 0\). The two-step comparator therefore takes the \(w_S = 0\) loadings and fits an unpenalized Cox model on the training program scores. It differs from the supervised fit only in whether survival entered the loadings and in how \(\beta\) was estimated.

1.5 Choosing the survival weight

The real-data fit uses \(w_S = 1\), fixed by five-fold training cross-validation (Section 4.1). Two refinements were tested in simulation. In the survival-block form, \(w_S\) multiplies the Cox term and the Kullback–Leibler term of \(\beta\) together, so \(\beta\) gets an ordinary Bayesian Cox fit while the loadings see survival at weight \(w_S\). The weight is chosen for each dataset from \(\{1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50\}\) by five-fold cross-validated partial log-likelihood, with ties going to the smaller weight. The same rule was applied to the real training data (Section 4.5).

1.6 The model behind the external results

Every external result in this version comes from the supervised YFB fit (\(w_S = 1\), 2,218 genes, rank 7) or its two-step comparator, and each external table and figure names its model in the caption. The supervised fit is fit_ssbmf_yfb(canonicalize = TRUE, w_S = 1) on the 2,218-gene set, with every RNA-seq cohort logged once and z-scored gene by gene within cohort, rank 7 without pruning, point-Laplace priors on \(L\) and \(F\) and a Normal prior on \(\beta\). The two-step comparator uses the same input and rank at \(w_S = 0\), followed by an unpenalized Cox fit (Section 1.4). The survival weight, the gene-set size and the choice not to screen genes on survival were fixed by training cross-validation. The gene screen, the input scaling and the rank were set earlier with external concordance (Section 2.2). If the analyses of Section 3 change the model, the results below keep this label, and the new model is scored once after it is fixed (Section 3.7).

2 Evaluation

2.1 Data

The model is trained on 273 patients (139 deaths) from two RNA-seq cohorts, TCGA-PAAD and CPTAC (Table 1). Every RNA-seq cohort is transformed once by \(\log_2(x+1)\). Genes are screened separately in each training cohort by the combined mean and variance rank of DeSurv (Young et al. 2026), keeping the top 3,000 per cohort. The screen uses no outcomes. The intersection, called the 2,218-gene set, has 2,218 genes. Each cohort is then standardized gene by gene to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The 5 external series supply 616 records and 414 recorded deaths. The PACA-AU array and RNA-seq series share 47 donors, and the RNA-seq series has 52 records from 51 donors, so the external collection represents 568 people if the other cohorts are distinct (counts from the October 16 accuracy review, paper/writeup/2026-10-16-writeup/_process/Accuracy_Review_Dispositions_10_16_26.md).

2.2 Uses of the external cohorts

Every modeling choice is made by simulation and by five-fold cross-validation on the 273 TCGA and CPTAC training patients. This includes preprocessing, gene screening, the priors, the rank, the survival weight and the tuning of comparators. The five external expression series (Dijk, Moffitt, PACA-AU array, PACA-AU RNA-seq and Puleo) and the matched ICGC methylation set only score a model after it is fixed. Their results are reported, but they never choose between models or settings. The DeSurv comparator used its published settings rather than a new search on our folds. The gene screen, the per-cohort standardization without a rank transform and rank 7 of the current model were set before this rule, using external concordance, and are being reselected on training cross-validation (Section 3.6). The audit in docs/findings/2026-11-06-external-cohort-uses.md records which earlier choices used which series.

The rule follows the protocol DeSurv used on the same cohorts (Young et al. 2026). DeSurv was trained on TCGA and CPTAC pooled. Every hyperparameter was chosen by five-fold cross-validation on the training data, with the one-standard-error rule for the rank, and the external cohorts were scored once with the final model. No portion of the training data is held out here either. With 273 patients, a held-out fifth would estimate concordance with a standard error near 0.05, larger than the differences between the settings being compared.

2.3 Simulation designs

All three simulation studies plant a single prognostic program among unsupervised structure and ask whether the fit recovers it. Recovery requires absolute loading correlation of at least 0.7, an active coefficient and the correct coefficient sign after loading alignment. A false-active program is one whose coefficient lies more than 1.96 posterior standard deviations from zero but which does not match the planted program.

  • The fixed-weight simulation. Survival weight at 2,000 genes. Data with 50 or 2,000 genes and a planted program explaining 0.25%, 1.00%, 5.00% of expression variance. We fitted 10 datasets per cell at \(w_S \in \{0, 1, 10, 100, 1{,}000, 10{,}000\}\), at \(w_S = p/50\) and at a weight calibrated to give survival 20% of the loading precision. The generator uses strong planted survival effects.
  • The cross-validated-weight simulation. The larger gene-count cells of the fixed-weight simulation plus a cell with weaker survival. The weight was chosen per dataset by the rule of Section 1.5. Two fits differ in the coefficient posterior. The block-weighted fit uses a mean-field posterior, with the survival weight multiplying the Cox term and the Kullback–Leibler term of \(\beta\). The joint-posterior fit is block-weighted with a joint Gaussian posterior for \(\beta\).
  • The near-threshold simulation. Programs near the detection threshold. Planted programs explained 0.05%, 0.10%, 0.20% of expression variance, with 10 datasets per cell. The mean oracle concordance ranges were 0.94 to 0.96 for strong survival and 0.73 to 0.74 for realistic survival.

The cross-validated-weight and near-threshold simulations compare the supervised and matched two-step fits on the same datasets. The unsupervised reference in the fixed-weight simulation was uncentered, so the matched two-step comparison on its cells comes from the cross-validated-weight simulation.

2.4 Performance metrics and uncertainty

Discrimination is Harrell’s concordance index C (Harrell et al. 1982), with the risk direction fixed from training. Paired differences between two models use percentile bootstrap intervals (Efron and Tibshirani 1993) from resampling patients within each cohort, with both models scored on the same resamples. The pooled difference is the equal-weight mean of the within-series differences. Calibration is the slope from a Cox regression of held-out survival on the fitted score. A slope above one indicates fitted risk differences that are too small. A slope below one indicates differences that are too large. In simulation the slopes use exact event times, because the default tie handling of survival::coxph() merges the extreme simulated times and flattens every slope.

The record bootstrap resamples records within series. The donor sensitivity resamples each donor together with every observed record, so the 47 donors shared by the two PACA-AU series move together. Both pooled intervals use the same equal-weight mean of the within-series differences.

3 Work of November 9–13

This section lists the analyses planned for the week of November 9. Each was registered, with its criteria, before any fit. Their results are in progress or pending review, so each subsection gives the question and a marked placeholder for the result. Unless a subsection says otherwise, the simulation cells are the three planted variance shares of the fixed-weight simulation (0.25%, 1% and 5% at 2,000 genes) and the near-threshold cell with a 0.05% share and strong survival. The real-data comparisons use the five training folds of Section 4.1, balanced by cohort and event. All fits keep rank 7 and the unit survival weight unless the subsection varies them. None of these analyses uses an external cohort to make a choice.

3.1 Priors on the scores and loadings

A nonnegative factorization, as in DeSurv, makes each program an additive set of genes. This comparison asks whether point-exponential priors on \(L\) and \(F\) recover a planted prognostic program as well as the working point-Laplace fit, with false activity and convergence under control, and whether they predict as well under training cross-validation. The point-exponential fit takes nonnegative input, each gene divided by its within-cohort standard deviation without centering, and centers the program scores that enter the Cox model. The point-Laplace fit takes the working z-scored input. Both arms are fitted to the pooled training data without cohort strata. Within-cohort concordance is the primary cross-validation metric, with pooled concordance reported beside it.

3.2 Prior on the survival coefficients

Under the \(L\) and \(F\) prior chosen above, this comparison asks which prior on \(\beta\) the working model should use: point-Laplace, point-normal or Normal. The working fit has used a Normal prior without a comparison that chose it. The three arms differ only in the \(\beta\) prior and use the same simulation cells and training folds. For the point-normal prior the posterior inclusion probability of each program is also recorded.

3.3 Methylation fitted alone

This analysis asks whether the single-modality model, fitted to methylation alone, finds prognostic programs that the expression fit does not. It uses the matched TCGA patients with expression, methylation and survival. CpGs with mean methylated fraction between 0.1 and 0.9 on these patients (182,934 CpGs) are ranked by variance, and the fit is run on the top 10,000, 25,000, 50,000 and 100,000 and on all of them. Both input and prior setups of Section 3.1 are fitted, with a Normal prior on \(\beta\). The comparison is with an expression fit on the same patients and folds. A methylation program counts as not seen in expression if its patient scores correlate below 0.5 with every expression program score and it is survival-active in the full fit and in at least three of five folds. With about 150 patients the concordance comparison is descriptive. A full fit at each count is timed first, and cross-validation runs only for counts that converge. If the comparison of \(\beta\) priors adopts a sparse prior, the methylation fits are repeated under it.

3.4 One fitter for several data types

This work asks whether one fitter, with shared scores \(L\) and a separate loading matrix and prior for each data type, can fit expression alone, methylation alone or both, and so replace the single-modality fitter. The first check is that its single-data-type path reproduces the single-modality fitter in \(E[L]\), \(E[F]\), \(E[\beta]\) and the final objective to a relative tolerance of \(10^{-6}\). Its Kullback–Leibler helpers are then checked against two properties of the single-modality objective: the Gaussian log-normalizer in the activity KL is counted once per observation, and the coefficient KL is exactly zero for a flat coefficient likelihood. A two-data-type simulation plants one shared prognostic program, and the real-data step fits expression, methylation and both on the matched TCGA patients with the folds of Section 3.3.

3.5 Survival through the scores or through the projection

The working model links survival to the projection of the data on the loadings, \(\eta = (YF)\beta\), and scores new patients by that projection. The alternative links survival to the latent scores, \(\eta = L\beta\), and scores new patients by fold-in, which solves for their scores under the stored priors. This comparison fits both on identical input, priors, starting values and folds, so only the parameterization of the hazard differs. It reports simulation recovery, training cross-validation, the programs of the two full fits and, as description only, the external scores of the two fixed models.

3.6 Training cross-validation of the gene screen, input scaling and rank

Three choices of the current model were set with external concordance (Section 2.2). Each is redone here by five-fold training cross-validation. Five outcome-free gene screens, labeled D1 to D5, are compared. D4 is the 2,218-gene screen of the working model. The input scalings compared are within-cohort z-scores, division by the within-cohort standard deviation, and a within-patient rank transform. One further fixed arm ranks genes within each patient, divides each gene by its within-cohort standard deviation and uses point-exponential priors. The rank is selected over \(K = 2, \dots, 12\) by the one-standard-error rule, with the number of programs with nonzero loadings and of survival-active programs reported at each \(K\).

4 Results

4.1 Supervised fit against the rank-7 two-step fit

On the training patients, the supervised fit had mean fold concordance 0.663 against 0.652 for the two-step fit (Table 2). The paired fold difference was +0.011 (SE 0.005). In 2 of the five folds the supervised fit reached the 300-sweep cap with the objective still changing slowly. Their coefficients were small, and no coefficient or noise precision was growing, so these folds showed no sign of divergence.

This configuration (\(w_S = 1\), the 2,218-gene set, no survival screen) was fixed from these training results before any external cohort was scored. It was then scored once on the five external series (Table 3). This is the supervised YFB fit (\(w_S = 1\), 2,218 genes, rank 7) of Section 1.6. Every external result in this section comes from it and its two-step comparator.

The supervised fit scored equal to or higher than the two-step fit in every series. Its mean external concordance was 0.620 and the two-step fit’s 0.613. The pooled paired difference was +0.007 (95% interval −0.002 to 0.017), and +0.006 (−0.003 to 0.016) without the PACA-AU RNA-seq series. The donor bootstrap interval is −0.003 to 0.017 for the full panel. All pooled intervals include zero. The difference is about the size of the training cross-validation difference. Dijk and Moffitt were the weakest series for both fits.

The supervised slope was closer to one in 4 of 5 series. In PACA-AU RNA-seq it was 1.57, compared with 1.26 for two-step. In Puleo it was 0.99.

As a summary on the scale DeSurv reports (Young et al. 2026), the hazard ratio per standard deviation of the risk score, from a Cox model stratified by series over all 616 records, was 1.37 (95% CI 1.24 to 1.51) for the supervised fit and 1.35 (1.22 to 1.49) for the two-step fit.

4.2 What survival does to the real-data loadings

On the training data at \(w_S = 1\), survival supplies between \(2 \times 10^{-10}\) and \(8 \times 10^{-7}\) of the loading precision (median over programs, across the gene-set sizes below). The simulation cell medians at the same weight ranged from 0.01 to 0.20 at the larger gene count. Two things keep it small on real data. The fitted coefficients are small (largest \(|\bar\beta_k|\) 0.41 per standard deviation of the program score), and the share scales with \(E[\beta_k^2]\). The real programs also explain much more expression variance than the planted programs in simulation, so their expression precision is large. The loading correlations between the fits round to 1.000 for every matched pair. The concordance difference in Section 4.1 reflects the joint coefficient update with its shrinkage prior.

Adding genes beyond the 2,218-gene set did not help (Table 4). Supervised concordance ranged from 0.643 to 0.663 across sizes, and every size was within one standard error of the others. The registered rule, which picks the smallest set within one standard error of the all-genes concordance whose survival-active programs match the all-genes fit at \(|r| \ge 0.7\), chose the 2,218-gene set for both fits. The supervised advantage over the two-step fit shrank as genes were added and reversed at larger gene-set sizes.

Screening genes on survival inside each training fold, by a cohort-stratified univariable Cox test, gave no consistent gain over an outcome-free screen of the same size: the paired differences were 0.001 to 0.021 across sizes and fits, each within about one paired standard error, and no screened set beat the supervised fit on all 2,218 genes. With survival permuted in simulated data, the \(w_S = 1\) fit had 0.1 to 0.5 false-active programs per dataset on average, below the registered limit of one.

4.3 Simulation: supervision strength and the weight choice

At \(w_S = 1\) with 2,000 genes the fit recovered the planted program in all 10 datasets per variance cell, with mean false-active counts 0.9, 0.1, 0.0, and every fit converged. No fit at a weight of 40 or greater converged at the larger gene count. Training CV selected the unit weight in 55 of 60 datasets. The coefficients at \(w_S = 1\) were attenuated: median validation calibration slopes were 1.45, 2.16, 3.23 across the three cells, where one denotes calibration. Mean validation concordance ranged from 0.944 to 0.986.

In the cross-validated-weight simulation the weights selected by partial log-likelihood increased with the planted signal (Table 5). Both supervised arms and the matched two-step fit recovered the planted program in every dataset. Mean validation concordance differed by at most 0.007. Each arm met the calibration band in 1 of 3 variance cells. The mean-field arm’s largest mean null false-active count at its modal weight was 1.1. Neither arm passed all criteria. The mean concordance of the joint and mean-field coefficient variants differed by at most 0.001.

4.4 Simulation: programs near the detection threshold

In the cells of the fixed-weight and cross-validated-weight simulations the two-step fit already finds the planted program, so those simulations cannot show what supervision adds. The near-threshold simulation planted weaker programs (Table 6). With strong survival the supervised fit had the higher validation concordance in 29 of 30 datasets, and the gain grew as the program weakened. At the smallest planted share, 0.05%, the supervised fit recovered the program in 5 of 10 datasets, where the two-step fit recovered none, and validation concordance rose by +0.156. With realistic survival the two fits were close at the larger shares, and neither recovered the program at the smallest share. The registered recovery criterion still failed in every strong cell, because it also required a mean of at most one false-active program per cell. The two-step fit had as many or more false-active programs in the same cells.

The post hoc analysis measures the variance of the sum of the nonmatched score contributions relative to the variance of the full score. It includes nonmatched programs below the survival-activity threshold. It also measures full-minus-matched concordance on the same datasets. In the cross-validated-weight simulation the largest cell median variance ratio was 0.8%, and the largest absolute cell mean change in concordance was 0.002. In the larger-share cells of the near-threshold simulation, the supervised (\(w_S = 1\), block-weighted) and two-step fits the corresponding ratios reached 1.3% for supervision and 2.9% for two-step. Across both fits the largest absolute mean change in C in those cells was 0.008. At the smallest planted share the median ratios ranged from 8.7% to 68.8%. These score summaries leave the registered false-active verdicts unchanged.

4.5 Real-data refit at the cross-validated weight

The largest cross-validated partial log-likelihood on the training folds occurred at \(w_S = 1\). Across the tested grid from 1 to 50, the criterion varied by 0.26. The nested folds selected weights 5, 2, 50, 1, 10. Nested cross-validation gave mean C 0.656 (SE 0.027), compared with 0.663 for the \(w_S = 1\) fit. At the largest tested weight the median survival share for active loadings was \(7.3 \times 10^{-5}\). The registered rule kept \(w_S = 1\), so the external results of Section 4.1 apply unchanged.

4.6 Rank and ELBO pruning

The pruning simulation asks whether ELBO pruning recovers the planted program and the true rank. For a flat coefficient likelihood the coefficient update returns the prior moments and an exact zero coefficient KL. Ordinary and protected pruning both failed the registered recovery and rank criteria (Table 8), so the fit retains all 7 starting columns.

4.7 Comparison with other prognostic models

Both comparisons were registered before they were run. The supervised and two-step scores in this section are those of the supervised YFB fit (\(w_S = 1\), 2,218 genes, rank 7) (Section 1.6). Every comparator was trained on the 273 training patients only, and each score’s direction was fixed on the training data. DeSurv used the authors’ code, preprocessing and published settings (rank 3), which the authors selected on the same training cohorts (Young et al. 2026). The elastic-net Cox model on the 2,218-gene set chose \(\alpha = 0\) by cross-validation on the training folds. The α = 0.75 and lasso paths reached glmnet’s iteration limit at small penalties. PurIST entered as a Cox model on its basal-like probability (Rashid et al. 2020). No clinical model was fitted, because no stage, grade, age or margin field is recorded in both training cohorts and all five external series.

Every paired concordance interval included zero (Table 9). Unsupervised EBMF followed by Cox regression gave differences, supervised fit minus EBMF, of +0.007, +0.045, +0.040 at ranks 7, 15 and 40. At ranks 15 and 40 the unpenalized Cox step overfit, with external calibration slopes of 0.10 to 0.49, so those differences describe that pipeline rather than the information in a larger factorization.

4.7.1 Risk groups from training cutpoints

One cutpoint per score maximized the log-rank statistic on the out-of-fold training scores, with at least 20% of patients per group. It was applied unchanged in every external series. The cutpoints were −0.046 training SDs for the supervised score and 0.526 for the two-step score. The pooled high-versus-low HRs were 1.52 (1.24 to 1.87) and 1.69 (1.32 to 2.16). They are not comparable, because the supervised cutpoint places 297 of 616 external records in the high-risk group and the two-step cutpoint places 144. A smaller, more extreme group gives a larger HR at equal ranking ability. After adjusting for PurIST subtype the supervised score’s pooled HR per training SD was 1.48, and after adjusting for DeCAF it was 1.40. Figure 6 displays the groups formed by the training cutpoints. The program section also gives within-series tertiles as a separate description of ranking. The out-of-fold scores used the feature matrix of the training fit, whose per-cohort scaling included held-out training-fold expression. The cutpoint search used the pooled out-of-fold training scores and their outcomes.

These fixed groups and the subtype-adjusted associations are exploratory. Differences between high-versus-low hazard ratios also reflect differences in the patients assigned to each group.

4.7.2 Program stability in training folds

A main prognostic program was defined before the analysis by a standardized coefficient at least 0.25 of the largest, at least 5% of the signed risk-score variance and survival activity in at least four of the five training folds.

Programs 2 and 3 met the rule. Program 5 met the coefficient and share thresholds but was active in only 3 folds. In the saved fits of the cross-validated-weight simulation the coefficient-and-share part kept the planted program in 80 of 80 fits and rejected 35 of 36 false-active directions. In the two-step fits of the near-threshold simulation it rejected 61 of 128. The fold-stability part could not be checked in simulation.

4.7.3 Mixed-signal simulation

A simulation planted one strong and one near-threshold prognostic program with equal standardized effects at 2,000 genes.

At \(w_S = 1\) the supervised and two-step fits recovered the near-threshold program equally often. A fixed \(w_S = 5\) lost it in most datasets and had lower validation C.

4.7.4 Recovery across simulation designs

The matched two-step fit recovered the planted program in the representative cell of the cross-validated-weight simulation. The largest unit-weight recovery difference in the near-threshold simulation favoured the supervised fit and occurred at the smallest planted share with strong survival (Table 6). In the mixed-signal simulation, the two unit-weight fits had the same near-threshold recovery as the two-step fit. Figure 7 shows the accompanying differences in false activity, convergence and calibration. On PDAC data the loading agreement and the small Cox contribution to loading precision are consistent with an effect through the coefficient fit (Section 4.2).

5 Programs of the supervised fit

The programs in this section are those of the supervised YFB fit (\(w_S = 1\), 2,218 genes, rank 7) (Section 1.6), and every external association reported here comes from that model. The joint fit retained 7 programs. Of those, 3 were survival-active (Table 12). Program 2 had a protective coefficient at its positive pole, where the leading genes included classical epithelial and exocrine markers. Its negative pole included hypoxia and glycolysis genes. Program 3 had an adverse coefficient at its ribosomal and proliferative pole. Program 5 also had an adverse coefficient, with enrichment of mitotic and stromal-immune signatures.

5.1 Enrichment and published signatures

Enrichment was calculated on signed loadings among the modeled genes. The leading sets are in Table 13. Program 3’s influenza-labeled sets share leading ribosomal genes in the saved enrichment results.

5 Reactome p-values were unestimable and are retained as missing in the source CSV. Spearman correlations with published signatures were computed within series using the available standardized expression genes. In the pooled training data, Programs 2 and 3 were inversely associated with the Moffitt basal-like and classical signatures, respectively. The corresponding external ranges are in Table 14. Correlations between Program 5 and the stromal-immune signature were weaker. These descriptive associations characterize fixed programs.

The loadings of the supervised fit and of the \(w_S = 0\) fit agreed at \(|r| = 1.000\) for every matched program (Section 4.2).

5.2 Evidence for the individual programs

Program 2 combines the clearest external direction agreement with survival activity in 5 training folds. Its protective pole is associated with classical epithelial and exocrine expression. Its adverse pole includes hypoxia and glycolysis genes. The separate external Cox estimates agree in direction with its training coefficient across all scored series.

Program 3 was active in 4 training folds. Its adverse pole includes ribosomal and proliferative genes, and its opposite pole correlates with the classical signature. The unadjusted external estimates generally follow the training direction (Table 15).

Program 5 had an adverse full-fit coefficient and enrichment for mitotic and stromal-immune signatures. It was active in 3 training folds. Its pooled external HR per training SD was 0.87 (donor-clustered 95% CI 0.76 to 1.00), opposite in direction to its training coefficient, and 3 of the 5 series had HRs below one. Its biological interpretation is exploratory. The retention rule in Section 4.7.2 reflects that instability.

5.3 External program associations and risk groups

Separate external Cox regressions give descriptive associations per series SD of each active program score. The numbers of estimates in the training direction, in program order, were 5, 4, 2 of 5. These estimates are marginal. The training coefficients condition on the other program scores.

Kaplan–Meier curves use within-series tertiles of the fixed risk score or fixed program scores of the supervised fit. Program scores are oriented using the training coefficients. The tertiles describe relative ranking within each series. They use a different set of cutpoints in each series.

6 Discussion

6.1 Interpretation

For the supervised YFB fit (\(w_S = 1\), 2,218 genes, rank 7), the external concordance difference was small and its interval included zero. The estimated loadings correlated 1.000 with the unsupervised loadings at the unit survival weight. DeSurv and elastic-net Cox trained on the same patients performed similarly. The joint coefficient fit accounts for posterior loading uncertainty and uses a shrinkage prior. Calibration slopes were closer to one in most series.

In the simulation cells with consistent recovery, the two-step fit already recovered the prognostic program. The near-threshold simulations isolated a setting where supervision could change discovery. Recovery and concordance improved when survival was strong, while the differences were smaller at realistic survival strength.

6.2 Limitations

The gene screen, the input scaling and the rank of the supervised YFB fit (\(w_S = 1\), 2,218 genes, rank 7) were chosen with external concordance before the training-only rule, and every external series informed at least one of the choices recorded in the audit (Section 2.2). The external results in this version therefore describe a model whose setup was partly chosen on the same cohorts. These choices are being reselected on training data (Section 3.6). The PACA-AU array and RNA-seq records both contribute to the pooled estimate. The donor bootstrap and the donor-clustered HR intervals account for their shared donors while retaining both series in the estimand. DeSurv used its published settings rather than a new search on our training folds. 2 of 5 supervised training folds stopped at the sweep cap. In simulation the coefficients at \(w_S = 1\) are attenuated at the larger gene count. These studies use a common simulation generator.

6.3 Continuing work

Proposed supervision weights include a calibrated power on the Cox partial likelihood, downweighting expression and normalizing the likelihood terms. Each would be assessed for recovery, calibration, false activity and convergence before application to the real data.

The analyses of Section 3 compare priors on the loadings and the coefficients, fit methylation alone, test a fitter for several data types with shared activities and separate loading priors, compare the model with the \(\eta = L\beta\) parameterization, and reselect the gene screen, input scaling and rank on training data. Once their results are reviewed, the working model is fixed on training data and scored once on the external cohorts (Section 3.7). Every later choice follows the training-only rule of Section 2.2.

Appendix A. Model derivation

The canonical single-modality procedure uses training expression \(Y\) and survival times and indicators. It returns posterior moments of \(L\), \(F\) and \(\beta\), gene precisions and the tracked variational objective.

  1. Center and scale the input according to the training preprocessing recipe. Initialize the factorization using a truncated singular value decomposition of the resulting \(Y\).
  2. Compute the posterior mean and variance of \(\eta\). Re-expand the Cox partial log-likelihood about the current mean predictor, using the diagonal curvature to obtain a working normal-means objective.
  3. For each program, update \(\beta_k\) using the first and second moments of \(YF_k\). Update \(L_k\) from the expression residual. Update the entries of \(F_k\) using both likelihood contributions and refresh the projected scores within the loading update. Use empirical Bayes normal-means fits for the prior parameters.
  4. Update the gene-specific noise precisions. Record the monitored objective including the weighted Cox term and the Kullback–Leibler terms. Rescale nonzero programs to unit training projection SD and check the relative change in the objective.
  5. In each external series, apply the fixed projection loadings and coefficients to the available training genes. Harrell’s concordance uses the direction learned from training survival.

The full derivation gives the update formulas, the balance of expression and survival information and the numerical checks. The companion verify_derivation.R evaluates individual updates against the expected objective.

Appendix B. Changes since the November 6 version

  • External cohorts. The external cohorts only score fixed models. Every modeling choice is made by simulation and training cross-validation (Section 2.2).
  • Model names. The model behind the external results is named by its configuration, and every external table and figure names it in the caption (Section 1.6).
  • Historical comparisons removed. This version compares the current model only with the rank-matched two-step fit, EBMF at ranks 15 and 40 followed by Cox, DeSurv, elastic-net Cox and PurIST. Removed: the pre-registered October 15 supervision check, the \(\alpha_F = 0\) benchmark and its single-log refit, the 40-factor LASSO comparator, the matches with historical loadings, the table of past external-cohort uses and the earlier multimodal appendix.
  • Work of November 9–13. Section 3 describes the week’s analyses with placeholders for their results.

No number retained from the November 6 version has changed.
